Subject: Urgent - Safety Hazard at 27A Ridgeway

Dear Sarah,

I am writing to bring to your attention a safety hazard at 27A Ridgeway. Following the recent high winds, Mr. Clarke has reported a loose balcony railing which poses a risk to the tenant's safety.

In the meantime, I intend to advise the tenant to avoid using the balcony until the repairs are complete.

Please let me know your instructions regarding this matter.

Best regards,
Aisha

Subject: Discovering Local History through Street Names

Dear New Residents,

As a local agent, I've had the pleasure of watching new families move into our community and settle into their new homes. As you explore your new neighborhood, you may have noticed the various street names that seem to hold a story or two. Many of these street names actually trace back to farms, landowners, or past local industries that played a significant role in shaping our town's history.

These street names serve as a reminder of the rich history and heritage that surrounds us. They not only provide a glimpse into the past but also serve as signposts or indicators of the local culture and traditions that have been passed down through generations.

During my walking tours, I love pointing out these street names and sharing the stories behind them with new residents. It's a great way to connect the dots between the present and the past, and to give you a deeper appreciation for the community you're now a part of.

I hope to see you on one of my upcoming tours!

Best regards,
Aisha Campbell

Subject: Competitive Offer Request for [Property Address]

Dear [Recipient's Name],

I hope this email finds you well. We have received multiple offers for the three-bedroom terrace at [Property Address], and we would like to invite you to submit a competitive offer to secure this popular property.

We look forward to receiving your offer and working with you to secure this property.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

Aisha

I am writing to inform you that the Mr and Mrs O'Neill's property at 18 Clifton Road has a maintenance issue that requires your attention. A cracked double-glazed unit in the living room is causing a draught and a minor security concern.

To proceed with the necessary repairs, I kindly request that you authorise the cost and advise whether to replace the whole frame or just the glazed unit. Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Best regards,
Aisha

Aisha

task_instruction: Advice on lease extension process where lease below 80 years
task_details: Buyer Oliver is buying a flat where the lease is 78 years. Explain implications for mortgages and resale, steps to instruct a specialist solicitor and surveyor, estimated timeframe and costs for a statutory lease extension, and whether to proceed before or after purchase. Provide clear next steps and offer recommendations.
personalized:
Hiya Oliver,

A lease under 80 years is important to flag. Lenders can be cautious and extending later can be more expensive, so it’s good to consider the options now.

First, get a specialist leasehold solicitor and a chartered surveyor to estimate the premium and likely legal costs for a statutory lease extension. Your solicitor will calculate the compensation owed to the freeholder and the surveyor will value the premium. The statutory process typically takes several months once started and can cost a few thousand pounds depending on the property and the remaining years.

You can choose to buy now and extend later, or negotiate for the seller to start the extension before exchange. If you plan to mortgage, check with your lender — some will lend with a lease under 80 years but may ask for a plan for extension. I can recommend local leasehold specialists who handle Enfield flats regularly.

Give me a bell if you want those recommendations or if you’d like me to ask the seller to start the extension process before exchange.

Best wishes,
Aisha

task_instruction: Landlord selling with tenants needing notice or transfer arrangements
task_details: Landlord Marcus is selling a property with tenants present and needs to either obtain vacant possession or transfer the tenancy to the buyer. Explain steps including giving tenant notice if required, solicitor coordination, deposit transfer details, and timelines. Clarify responsibilities and offer to liaise with tenants.
personalized:
Hiya Marcus,

Thanks — selling with tenants in place is common and we’ll make sure it’s handled properly. First, confirm whether you and the buyer have agreed on vacant possession or that the tenancy will transfer on completion. If vacant possession is required your solicitor will advise on the correct notice period and paperwork. If the tenancy transfers, your solicitor must provide deposit protection details and the AST so the buyer’s solicitor can record the tenancy.

Next, please ensure the tenant’s deposit protection certificate and contact details are provided to the buyer’s solicitor before exchange. Your solicitor will coordinate the legal transfer of the AST or prepare the paperwork for a vacate notice. Timelines vary, but allow at least two to four weeks to serve notices and provide the necessary documentation.

If you’d like, I can speak with the tenants to reassure them and explain the process. Give me a bell and I’ll arrange a suitable time to visit.

Best,
Aisha

Dear Home Buyers,

As a local agent, I'm delighted to share with you the rich history of the Lea Valley, which has significantly influenced the development of our neighbourhoods. Market gardening, which once thrived in this area, has left an enduring legacy that makes our community a unique and desirable place to live.

The long plots and areas of greenery created by market gardening were later transformed into the suburban streets we know today. While much has changed over the years, physical remnants of this past remain, including allotments and street names that pay homage to the area's agricultural heritage. These subtle nods to the Lea Valley's history are a testament to the community's enduring connection to the natural world.

For families seeking easy access to green space, the Lea Valley's historical character is a major selling point. The area's proximity to parks, gardens, and the river Lea itself offers a tranquil escape from urban life, making it an ideal choice for those who value a balance between city living and outdoor recreation.

If you're considering making the Lea Valley your home, I'd be happy to show you the area's hidden gems and explain how this unique history has shaped the community we live in today.

task_instruction: Break down a fixtures and fittings clause for a buyer
task_details: Clause reads: 'All fixtures and fittings are included except those specifically excluded in the attached inventory: chandelier in dining room, freestanding fridge, and personal items.' Explain what 'fixtures' and 'fittings' mean, how to interpret the inventory, and what to do if a disputed item is still in the property at completion.
personalized:
Hiya,

In plain terms, fixtures are items fixed to the property (for example, built-in kitchen units), and fittings are movable items (like a freestanding fridge). First, look at the attached inventory: anything listed as excluded is not part of the sale and the seller should take it. Everything else stays with the property.

If a dispute happens — say the chandelier shows up at completion but the seller believes it was excluded — the first step is to check the signed contract and the inventory attachment. If the item is not excluded there, it should remain for you after completion. If the seller removes something they were supposed to leave, we can raise it with their solicitor and seek a remedy; often this is resolved before completion.

Practical tip: before completion arrange a quick walk-around with me so we can check the agreed items are in place. If you want, I can prepare a short checklist showing the items you expect to remain.

Speak soon,
Aisha

- Definitions/examples: fixtures = items fixed to the property (example: built-in kitchen units); fittings = movable items (example: freestanding fridge).
- Key factual points about the sale:
  - Any item listed as "excluded" in the attached inventory is not part of the sale and the seller should take it.
  - All other items on the inventory remain with the property.
- Steps if there is a dispute about an item (example: chandelier):
  - First check the signed contract and the inventory attachment.
  - If the item is not listed as excluded, it should remain for the buyer after completion.
  - If the seller removes something they were supposed to leave, the buyer’s solicitor can raise the issue with the seller’s solicitor and seek a remedy; these issues are often resolved before completion.

  - Arrange a quick walk-around before completion with the sender to check agreed items are in place.
  - Sender can prepare a short checklist showing the items the buyer expects to remain.

task_instruction: Advice for completion falling on a Friday and bank timings
task_details: Completion is set for Friday. Explain bank transfer times, the possible effect on key release, recommend earlier time or contingency if keys needed same day, and outline who is responsible for confirming cleared funds. Keep tone practical and local.
personalized:
Hiya both,

A quick note because completion is on a Friday. Banks often process large transfers earlier in the day but some systems close sooner on Fridays, which can delay the confirmation that funds have cleared.

First, I suggest agreeing an earlier completion time on the day so there’s the best chance your funds are processed and keys can be released by mid-afternoon. Your solicitor will confirm when the funds have cleared and then instruct the release of keys. If you absolutely need keys on the day but funds might take longer, ask the seller if they’ll agree to hold the keys overnight with agreed ID checks — we’ll only do this with solicitor confirmation.

I’ll coordinate with both solicitors the day before to set a realistic time and keep everyone posted. Give me a bell if you want me to request an earlier slot from solicitors.

Best,
Aisha

Subject: Shared Paving Area - Let's Organize a Quick Tidy-Up

Dear Neighbours,

I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to bring to your attention the shared paving area that connects our homes, which has become increasingly mossy and slippery during wet weather. As you can appreciate, this poses a safety concern for us all, especially our children and elderly residents.

I was thinking it would be great if we could organize a small tidy-up day to address this issue. I propose we use a pressure washer or a moss treatment/solution to restore the paving to its original condition. I'm happy to supply the necessary materials and assist with the work.

Best regards,
Aisha

task_instruction: Responding to survey findings and negotiating a solution
task_details: After a homebuyer survey reported damp in the cellar and some roof tiles loose, buyer wants to negotiate. Provide options: request seller repairs before exchange, reduced price, or a contribution to remedial works; outline who arranges quotes, timescales for decisions, and next steps. Keep tone collaborative and practical.
personalized:
Hiya,

Thanks for sending the survey report. The damp in the cellar and the loose roof tiles are things we can work with. Here are sensible options and how we’ll approach them.

First, we can ask the seller to carry out the repairs before exchange. That means getting a quote and setting a deadline for the work to be done and signed off. Second, we can ask for a price reduction or a completion-day contribution to cover the remedial costs; we’d need a couple of quotes to back up the amount. Third, if the works are minor you may accept them and have your builder do them after completion with a reduced price.

If you’d like me to, I can request two local tradespeople to provide quotes within 5–7 days so we have firm numbers to negotiate with the seller. Tell me which option you prefer and I’ll take it from there.

Give me a bell and we’ll decide the best route together.

Warmly,
Aisha
